title: Found
description:
An accommodation search that helps you research places, find them on the map, and contact them.





## Found

Found helps you look for accommodation and follow up on places that interest you. Describe what you need, and it researches candidates with sources you can check. Each result shows how it fits your requirements and which details still need confirming.

I put a lot of work into the design and how everything connects. You can open a candidate directly in the conversation, look through its photos, then explore the map to see what your commute would be like. I wanted moving through the results to feel easy, with enough detail to help you decide whether a place is worth contacting.

When you find somewhere you like, you can ask Found to draft an email about it, including questions the research couldn’t answer. You review the draft before sending, and replies arrive in the app’s inbox. Making that step from “I like this place” to “I’ve contacted them” feel quick and completing that loop easily was a big part of the work.

## Why I made it

The idea came from my own accommodation search. I’m hoping to do my bachelor’s thesis in Germany, and I wanted something I could use to help find somewhere to stay.

## How it’s built

Convex handles the backend and realtime updates, and hosts the frontend. Found uses its Agent, Auth, and Static Hosting components, among others, along with the Firecrawl and AgentMail Convex components.

- **OpenAI** powers the agent’s reasoning and tool use, including follow-up questions and email drafting.
- **Firecrawl** searches for accommodation and reads listing pages to gather information and supporting sources.
- **AgentMail** sends emails after approval and receives replies for the in-app inbox.
- **Google Maps** provides the interactive maps, commute routes, and Street View.

[Watch the walkthrough](https://youtu.be/ApUeWdys44Q) · [More about the design](https://adamamr.me/projects/found)

title: workshop
description:
Stop memorizing how the world works. Start experimenting, breaking things, and learning why they work.





# Workshop

**Stop memorizing how the world works. Start experimenting, breaking things, and learning why they work.**

The idea came from something I struggled with in school: I could memorize formulas and concepts, but I didn't always get the chance to actually experiment with them.

Physics, chemistry, and other practical subjects made much more sense when I could see what was actually happening instead of only reading about it.

So I wanted to build something where students could actually **experiment and learn by doing**.

This is **Workshop**.

## 1\. Problem

A lot of practical learning still happens through textbooks, diagrams, and formulas.

You can memorize that

```
F = ma
```

, learn a chemical equation, or read about how an orbit works — but that doesn't necessarily mean you understand what happens when you actually change the variables.

The bigger problem is access.

Not every student has access to a physics lab, chemistry equipment, CAD software, or the resources needed to experiment freely.

Workshop turns those concepts into something students can **touch, change, break, and try again**.

## 2\. How the app works

Workshop is a virtual hands-on laboratory with **39 experiments across 4 labs**.

The student chooses an experiment, changes its parameters, runs it, observes the result, and experiments again.

The four labs are:

- **CAD — Design & Engineering:** Build and manipulate 3D models and run load/stress simulations.
- **Physics — Mechanics & Waves:** Experiment with motion, forces, oscillations, collisions, waves, buoyancy, and more.
- **Chemistry — Elements, Molecules & Reactions:** Explore elements, build molecules, simulate reactions, and work with pH and titration.
- **Earth & Climate — Live Planetary Data:** Explore weather, air quality, earthquakes, oceans, climate, Earth imagery, astronomy, and planetary simulations.

Physics alone contains 12 experiments, including pendulum, projectile motion, free fall, springs, collisions, waves, buoyancy, Hooke's Law, and Newton's Laws.

Chemistry includes 11 experiments ranging from the periodic table and molecule building to reaction simulation, pH, titration, and concentration.

Earth & Climate combines live public data with local simulations, including weather, air quality, earthquakes, ocean conditions, climate trends, NASA imagery, astronomy, the Solar System, gravity, and tides.

## 3\. Notable features

### Real interactive experiments

These aren't pages explaining how an experiment works.

Students can actually change variables and observe the consequences.

For example, the Physics lab lets students change pendulum length, mass, gravity, damping, and starting angle while measuring the resulting period.

The physics engine uses a fixed-step **RK2 integrator running at 120 Hz**, decoupled from the rendering loop.

### AI Workshop Companion

Every lab has a contextual AI companion.

It doesn't simply receive:

> "Why did this happen?"

It receives the actual experiment context.

Workshop sends three layers:

- ```
stateSummary
```

— a plain-English description of the current state
- ```
paramDefs
```

— parameter names, labels, units, ranges, and options
- ```
state
```

— the complete raw experiment state

This prevents the model from having to guess what values such as

```
reaction=5
```

actually represent.

### AI + Web research

When MiniMax-M3 isn't confident about an answer, Workshop can trigger Firecrawl to retrieve external information and then give that information back to the model for the final explanation.

The system can retrieve up to three sources and records when Firecrawl was used.

### Persistent conversations

AI conversations are stored in Convex.

Each interaction keeps the experiment snapshot that was active when the question was asked, so the conversation remains connected to what the student was actually doing.

### Live data

The Earth & Climate lab uses live public data from sources including Open-Meteo, USGS FDSN, NASA POWER, NASA EPIC, and NASA APOD.

## 4\. Why did you build this?

I built Workshop because I wanted to create the kind of learning environment I wished I had more access to.

Reading about something and actually experimenting with it are two very different experiences.

I wanted students to be able to change a value, run an experiment, get an unexpected result, figure out why it happened, change something else, and try again.

That's the core idea behind Workshop:

**BUILD → EXPERIMENT → BREAK → CHANGE → TRY AGAIN → UNDERSTAND**

The goal isn't to replace real laboratories.

It's to make experimentation accessible when the real equipment, software, or laboratory isn't available.

## 5\. Tech stack

- **React** — application interface
- **TypeScript / JavaScript** — application logic
- **Convex** — backend, realtime state, persistence, and AI conversations
- **Three.js / React Three Fiber** — 3D experiments and CAD
- **MiniMax-M3** — Workshop Companion
- **GMI Cloud** — AI model infrastructure
- **Firecrawl** — contextual web research
- **Canvas** — physics simulations
- **Open-Meteo** — weather, air quality, marine and historical climate data
- **USGS FDSN** — earthquake data
- **NASA POWER** — solar and environmental data
- **NASA EPIC** — live Earth imagery
- **NASA APOD** — astronomy content

## 6\. Challenges we ran into

### Making AI understand raw experiment state

One of the hardest parts wasn't connecting an LLM.

It was making the model understand what the experiment state actually meant.

Raw state can contain values such as:

```
reaction = 5
body_A = 2
```

Those values are useful to the application but meaningless without context.

The solution was to build a context layer that translates the state into plain English and provides the model with labelled parameters, units, available options, and the raw state.

The model is explicitly instructed to read the human-readable state first instead of guessing.

### Keeping AI grounded

The AI should explain the experiment — not invent it.

The simulation remains the source of truth.

The model receives the actual experiment state and explains what happened based on that state.

### Building many different experiments

Workshop isn't one simulation with different labels.

It currently contains **39 experiments across four different domains**, each with different interaction models, data, calculations, and visualizations.

Building a common architecture that could support all of these while keeping each experiment independent was another major challenge.

Workshop started from a simple problem I experienced myself: **knowing the theory isn't always the same as understanding it.**

So I built a place where students can stop memorizing for a moment and actually experiment.

**Don't just learn how the world works. Try changing it.**

title: Bidzy
description:
An agent that helps homeowners email contractors for quotes, reads what comes back, and finds the real cheapest price.





## Problem

Getting a fair price on a job usually means emailing several companies and waiting for quotes to come back. A homeowner needs a new roof. A family needs a caterer for a wedding. A small business needs a moving company or a plumber or a contractor for an office fit out. Anyone in this position ends up doing the same slow, manual thing. Most people never actually do it properly because it is tedious and there is no good tool for it.

Even when someone does collect a few quotes, comparing them is harder than it sounds. The cheapest quote is often not the cheapest job. One company might exclude delivery. Another might leave out removal of old materials, or skip tax, or quietly exclude a scope item another contractor included. On paper the lowest number wins. Once everything that was left out gets added back in, it might actually be the most expensive option. Nobody does that math by hand. They just pick the lowest number and hope it holds up.

This is not a niche problem. It is something almost every homeowner and almost every small business owner runs into more than once.

## How it works

Bidzy gives each job its own real email inbox powered by AgentMail. Whoever is being contacted, a roofer, a caterer, a plumber, a moving company, never signs up for anything or installs anything. They just reply to an email like they normally would.

Once emailed, contractors reply however they want. A clean structured quote. A scanned PDF. A short messy reply typed on a phone between jobs. Bidzy reads all three and turns them into the same structured format so they can be compared fairly.

Bidzy then builds a comparable cost for each quote. It looks at what other contractors included for the same job and adds those costs back into any quote that left them out. A quote that looks cheaper because it silently excludes delivery gets corrected before you ever see the ranking.

If a reply comes from an email address Bidzy has not seen before, it does not guess. It flags the message for review instead of misattributing it.

If the job scope changes, Bidzy invalidates any quote that no longer applies and re ranks what is left, so you are never comparing prices against a job that does not exist anymore.

Every morning, a scheduled function checks who has not replied yet and sends a natural follow up automatically. No manual chasing required.

## Who this is for

A homeowner getting a roof replaced or a kitchen renovated. A couple planning a wedding and collecting caterer quotes. A small business owner sourcing a moving company, a cleaning service, or a contractor for office work. Anyone who would normally send the same request to several companies by email and then have to sit down and work out which reply is actually the best deal.

## Notable features

A real dedicated inbox per job through AgentMail, so the other side interacts with a normal email thread and nothing else.

Structured parsing of both PDF quotes and plain text replies into one consistent format.

Automatic comparable cost calculation that corrects for missing line items so the cheapest quote on paper does not automatically win.

License verification for contractors checked against public records.

Unknown sender detection that flags unmatched replies instead of silently misassigning them.

Fully automated daily follow ups running on Convex scheduled functions with no server or cron job to maintain.

Scope change handling that invalidates stale quotes and re ranks the remaining valid ones.

## Why we built this

Getting multiple quotes only helps if you can trust the comparison between them, and that trust breaks the moment two quotes are not actually pricing the same thing. Nobody manually reconciles what each company did or did not include, so the winning number is usually just whichever one was written lowest, correct or not.

We used roofing quotes as the concrete example because it is something almost every homeowner eventually deals with and gets wrong in exactly this way. The same problem shows up for weddings, moves, office work, and any situation where a homeowner or a small business would normally collect a few quotes by email.

## Technical overview

Bidzy is built entirely on Convex, using it for the database, backend functions, and scheduled jobs. There is no separate server and no cron infrastructure. A Convex scheduled function runs daily, checks the state of every job, and triggers follow up emails for anyone who has not responded.

AgentMail provides a real, isolated email inbox for each job. Outbound emails and inbound replies are both handled through AgentMail, and inbound replies trigger Convex functions that parse and process the message as soon as it arrives.

Firecrawl is used in two ways. It extracts structured data from PDF quote documents attached to email replies, and it performs contractor license lookups against public records for verification.

Quote parsing runs a comparison layer that normalizes line items across quotes, detects which costs are present or absent in each one, and calculates an adjusted comparable total. This is what powers the ranking shown on the dashboard.

The frontend is a React dashboard that displays live quote status, comparable cost rankings, and follow up activity per job.

## Challenges we ran into

Getting the comparable cost logic right was the hardest part. Different companies describe the same scope of work in very different language, so detecting whether a quote truly excludes something versus simply did not mention it took real iteration. Parsing casual, unstructured replies without losing detail or inventing detail that was not there was a constant balance. Tuning the automated follow up cadence so it felt like a helpful reminder rather than a spam bot also took a few passes.

## Results

A working end to end flow that a homeowner or a small business owner could actually use today. Real inboxes sending and receiving live email. Real quote parsing from both documents and plain text. Automatic comparable cost ranking that changes which quote wins once hidden exclusions are accounted for. A fully scheduled daily follow up system running entirely on Convex with no manual intervention required.

title: Subzero
description:
Know what’s renewing. Know how to stop it.





## The Problem

People sign up for free trials and subscriptions, then forget to cancel them before renewal. Others make what they think is a one-time purchase, only to discover later that it renews or converts into a recurring charge.

The problem isn't just remembering that a subscription exists. It's knowing **when you'll be charged, why you're being charged, where to cancel, and exactly how to stop it.**

## How SubZero Works

SubZero is an AI subscription protection tool.

Users can connect their email and SubZero automatically scans for subscription receipts, free trials, payment confirmations, and renewal-related emails.

For each subscription, SubZero:

1. **Identifies the subscription**: Extracts the merchant, price, trial period, renewal date, and other relevant details.
2. **Checks the merchant**: Uses Firecrawl to find current cancellation instructions, refund policies, and relevant terms.
3. **Understands the information**: OpenAI turns emails and web content into structured, actionable subscription data.
4. **Tracks renewals**: Convex stores subscription state, handles realtime updates, and runs scheduled workflows for renewal tracking and reminders.
5. **Alerts users when action is needed**: Users can see upcoming renewals and review what they need to do.
6. **Helps users cancel**: SubZero provides the exact cancellation route and can send cancellation requests through AgentMail when email cancellation is supported.

Users who don't want to connect their inbox can also forward individual subscription emails to SubZero.

## Notable Features

- Automatic subscription discovery from connected email
- Free trial and renewal detection
- Current merchant cancellation instructions
- Cancellation and refund policy analysis
- Renewal countdowns and reminders
- Actionable cancellation routes
- Email-based cancellation requests where supported
- Evidence-backed subscription information

## Why We Built It

Subscription trackers usually answer:

> "What subscriptions do I have?"

We wanted to answer the more useful question:

> **"I know I need to stop this charge. What exactly do I do?"**

SubZero is designed to move beyond simply tracking subscriptions and help users take action before an unwanted renewal happens.

## Tech Stack

- **Convex**: Backend, database, realtime state, queries, mutations, scheduled workflows, and production hosting
- **OpenAI**: Subscription extraction, information understanding, and policy interpretation
- **Firecrawl**: Merchant website and cancellation-policy discovery
- **AgentMail**: Receiving forwarded subscription emails and sending cancellation requests where supported
- **Next.js / React**: Frontend application

## Challenges

One of the biggest challenges was dealing with the fact that subscription and cancellation information is rarely structured consistently.

Different merchants use different renewal terms, cancellation flows, refund policies, and support channels. We therefore designed SubZero to distinguish between verified information and situations where a cancellation route cannot be confidently determined, rather than simply guessing.

Keeping cancellation information current is another challenge, which is why SubZero checks merchant websites instead of relying only on previously stored instructions.

## Success / Progress

We built a working end-to-end flow that can:

- Discover subscription information from email
- Extract structured subscription details
- Find and analyze merchant cancellation information
- Store and track subscriptions with Convex
- Display upcoming renewals and actionable cancellation information
- Support email-based cancellation workflows where applicable

The core MVP flow is:

**Connect email → discover subscription → verify cancellation path → track renewal → prompt the user to act.**

title: RecallReady
description:
Forward a receipt. RecallReady identifies the product, watches official recalls, and guides your household to safety.





Problem

Product recalls often fail to reach the people who need them. Families are expected to remember every model they own, repeatedly search fragmented safety websites, determine whether a notice applies to their exact product, and understand what action to take.

RecallReady reverses that burden by turning purchase emails into continuous household product protection.

How RecallReady works

1. A household saves its verified sender email in RecallReady.

2. The user forwards a real receipt or order confirmation to the household's private AgentMail inbox.

3. AgentMail sends a signature verified webhook to the Convex backend.

4. OpenAI extracts the product name, brand, model, retailer, category, purchase date, and other useful details.

5. Convex creates the inventory record and synchronizes the household dashboard in real time.

6. Firecrawl retrieves official product safety information used by the matching workflow.

7. RecallReady compares the household's exact brand and model against the safety notice.

8. When a match is found, the household sees the authority, hazard, official source, affected model, confidence, and recommended remedy.

9. AgentMail can send the evidence backed safety alert, while the household tracks the action through resolution.


Notable features

Real AgentMail email to inventory workflow

Signature verified inbound webhook processing

Sender to household email routing

OpenAI structured receipt and order email extraction

Firecrawl backed official source retrieval

Exact brand and model recall matching

Explainable match confidence and evidence

Realtime Convex inventory and activity updates

Searchable household product inventory

Product creation, editing, and deletion

Recall remedy and resolution tracking

Evidence backed outbound safety alerts

Household scoped authorization

Responsive desktop and mobile interface

Public frontend hosted with Convex static hosting

Why I built it

People already receive receipts and order confirmations, so RecallReady does not require them to develop a new safety habit. Forwarding an email creates a lasting record of that product and gives parents, partners, and caregivers one shared place to understand and resolve safety issues.

RecallReady is not another recall search box. It remembers what a household owns and makes official warnings personal, understandable, and actionable.

Tech stack

Convex: database, schema, validators, indexed queries, mutations, actions, internal functions, HTTP actions, full text search, scheduled processing, realtime subscriptions, audit events, and static frontend hosting

OpenAI: structured extraction of product information from real receipt and order email content

Firecrawl: retrieval of official product safety source information

AgentMail: private household inbox, inbound receipt delivery, signed webhooks, and outbound safety alerts

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, and Lucide

Build agent: OpenAI Codex with the Convex plugin

Challenges

The most significant challenge was creating a real email workflow rather than a pre populated demonstration. The webhook needed signature verification, idempotent processing, secure sender to household routing, and useful failure handling.

Another challenge was handling the raw OpenAI Responses API correctly. Structured response content needed to be read from the response output array rather than relying on SDK only convenience properties.

The matching workflow also needed to avoid vague AI generated warnings. RecallReady therefore exposes the exact model evidence, source authority, confidence, hazard, and official remedy.

Success and verification

Verified a real AgentMail email to inventory round trip in production

Verified OpenAI product extraction in production

Verified Firecrawl official source retrieval in production

Verified Convex realtime inventory and activity updates

Deployed publicly on Convex static hosting

Public GitHub repository with a complete hackathon.md build log

11 automated tests passing

Typecheck, lint, and production build passing

Zero known npm vulnerabilities

Final demonstration runtime: 2 minutes 20 seconds
review_note: Already models households, products, official recall matches, events and inbound emails. Shared household inventory alone is not distinctive.
tagline: Forward a receipt. RecallReady identifies the product, watches official recalls, and guides your household to safety.

title: Pigeon
description:
A newsletter for pages that don't have one. Watch any web page, get a plain-language email when it really changes.





The pages a family actually needs to watch never write back: the school's notice board, the embassy's appointment page, the building's announcements, a clinic's schedule, a government fee table. No RSS, no mailing list. People reload them, or miss the change. Pigeon checks a page on a schedule and emails your household or small team only when something meaningful changed, in two plain sentences, with the difference one click away.

TRY IT IN ABOUT A MINUTE, NO SIGN-UP

Open [https://marvelous-dinosaur-465.convex.site](https://marvelous-dinosaur-465.convex.site/) and press "Try it now". You get a real board. The first card is a demo: a fictional community notice board served by the app and watched through the real pipeline. Save an email if you want to receive the alert (optional; without one you still see every step and the reason no mail was sent). Then:

1. Firecrawl captures the original notice.
2. "Publish a cosmetic edit" rewords one sentence and bumps the timestamp and visitor counter. Pigeon logs it as cosmetic and sends nothing. That silence is the product.
3. "Publish a fee and deadline change" moves the fee from AED 1,000 to 1,500, the deadline from 15 to 10 October, and adds a closure. Within about half a minute you see the two-sentence summary, the judgment "money, dates or availability", the email status, and the diff.

A four-step progress line on the row shows captured, published, judged, emailed as they happen. Or paste any public page you care about; a Hacker News front page, re-checked ninety seconds later, was summarised as normal feed activity and correctly not emailed.

WHY SOMEONE KEEPS USING IT

• Only real changes reach you. Timestamps, counters, cache tokens and "last updated" lines are normalised away before comparison. What remains is judged: a decision model returns importance 1 to 5 with a confidence, the probability the change deserves an email, and whether it touches what you said you care about ("fees or deadlines"). Cosmetic changes are logged, not sent.
• A page that keeps changing does not keep nagging. After three alerts from one page in a day, the decision model is shown the last three alerts and asked whether the new change is materially different from all of them. A rewording, or a page flipping back to a state already reported, is logged with the reason instead of emailed.
• Every alert links to the diff of the captured text, colour-coded, so you never take the summary on faith.
• Households and small teams share a board, live: one person adds the page, everyone with an email saved gets the alert.
• Email works both ways. Send a link to the board's address from the email you saved, optionally with "hourly" or "daily" in the text, and Pigeon starts watching and replies with what it is now watching.

WHAT HAPPENS ON EVERY CHECK

URL and interval (30 minutes to weekly) → Firecrawl scrape to clean markdown with maxAge: 0 so a cached copy never masks a change → normalise → hash and compare with the previous snapshot (its hash recomputed with the current rules, so a rule change never looks like a page change) → store the snapshot and a byte-capped unified diff → decision model and language model run in parallel → alert if warranted → delivery status reconciled with the mail service for six hours. Checks are claimed with a token so the cron and "Check now" never scrape the same page twice, and a superseded worker cannot write. Error pages (HTTP 400 and up) never replace a good baseline.

HOW THE SPONSOR STACK DOES REAL WORK

• CONVEX: the whole backend. Schema with indexes, live queries on every screen, mutations, internal actions, HTTP actions, a five-minute cron and a daily one, scheduled functions (immediate first check, demo timers, six status syncs per email), Convex Auth with anonymous and password providers, three registered components, and the frontend served from convex.site by the static-hosting component.
• FIRECRAWL (@firecrawl/firecrawl-convex): every check is a real scrape with onlyMainContent and Firecrawl's own changeTracking verdict alongside Pigeon's diff.
• AGENTMAIL (@agentmail/convex): one inbox for the deployment. Sends the alerts with a reconciled delivery status, receives links through the signed webhook, routes them to the sender's board by address, refuses to guess when an address is on more than one board and the subject names none, and replies.
• OPENAI: openai/gpt-5.6-luna writes the two-sentence summary through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (OpenRouter). A separate decision model, typesafe/jev-1.13, returns the typed importance judgments. A heuristic covers both when a key is missing or a call times out.

WHAT BROKE, AND WHAT CHANGED

• The number normaliser was too eager: it replaced every comma-formatted number to suppress visitor counters, which would have hidden "AED 1,000" becoming "AED 1,500". It now only touches numbers next to a counter label, and old snapshots are re-hashed with the current rules.
• Convex components do not inherit the deployment's environment. The AgentMail component read its key without declaring it, so every send failed on the cloud deployment. A patch-package fix declares and binds the key; production installs apply it.
• The shared demo page rewrote itself every ten minutes by design, and a test board with a real email received 26 alerts in a morning. The page now rotates every six hours, finished demos fall back to a six-hour interval, unpublished demos relax after an hour, and the fatigue gate above exists because of it.
• A "Check now" click straight after publishing showed a raw "Server Error", because Convex hides plain error text in production. User-facing errors are now ConvexErrors with readable text, and timing conditions return a state instead of throwing.
• Two bugs were found by a seeded random-walk test that behaves like an impatient stranger (odd click orders, double clicks, junk URLs, malformed links, a second tab): a mistyped board id dropped the whole view to an error boundary, and a raw Firecrawl error string was shown in a watch row. Both fixed; the walk runs clean on multiple seeds after every deploy.

LIMITS AND RESOURCE CONTROLS

25 pages per board, 5 boards per owner, checks no more often than every 30 minutes (10 minutes only for the demo page, for its first hour), and a deployment-wide budget of 700 scrapes a day. Boards where nobody saved an alert email have their pages paused after a day, with a note and a one-click resume. Guest boards do not migrate to a later password account; the invite link is the way to bring a real account onto a board.

HONEST LIMITS

Pages behind logins or heavy bot protection may not scrape. The importance judgment is a model's call, not a guarantee: a ten-case filter smoke test and a six-case novelty smoke test behaved as expected, and both are narrow by design. Alert addresses are not confirmed by a verification mail; inbound routing requires SPF or DKIM to pass and refuses ambiguous cases, which is a mitigation, not ownership proof. Summaries are not automatically checked against the source sentence by sentence; the diff is there so you can.

LINKS

title: Jamanyo
description:
Jamanyo is an AI car scout that only calls a listing a lead when the evidence backs it up, with email delivery built on AgentMail.



## Problem

Car YouTubers I follow keep saying the same thing: finding the right car to buy takes weeks. You check scattered marketplaces by hand, work out what each price means (asking price, live bid, or a market benchmark), and sort real listings from editorial pages and closed auctions. Existing tools either need deep taxonomy knowledge or return noise from broad searches.

## How it works

Describe the car you want. It can be an explicit brief ("E46 M3, manual, under $35K") or a plain-language feeling ("analogue weekend car, learning-oriented ownership appetite").

1. **Firecrawl** searches a ranked registry of sources (Bring a Trailer, Classic.com, Hemmings) and scrapes individual listing pages.
2. An LLM assessment checks availability, price, and evidence quality.
3. A **deterministic evidence gate** decides what becomes a lead. Only a specific, available, inspectable listing with an explicit price qualifies. Market pages, editorial content, and closed auctions stay in a collapsed Research Trail.
4. A reactive **Convex** dashboard shows every mission, source, and activity event live.
5. **AgentMail** carries the email side: inbound requests arrive by signed webhook, and replies go out in the same thread.

**Current access:** Jamanyo is designed to be used from your inbox, but per-user agent inboxes need a higher AgentMail plan than I have. Today, anyone can sign up and use the full dashboard and join the email waitlist. The email flow runs through one controlled demo inbox, which the demo video shows.

## Notable features

- **Email-first design:** Svix-verified AgentMail webhooks, sender ownership checks, message deduplication, and threaded replies
- **Two discovery modes:** known-car briefs and guided discovery (plain language turned into up to three transparent search "lanes" with per-lane results)
- **Source-aware price semantics:** each source declares what its price means (asking price, current bid, buy-now, or market context), and the dashboard labels it accordingly
- **Deterministic closed-auction guard** that overrides model output
- **Auction Watch:** a single public listing, a silent first snapshot, and alerts only on material changes or deadline milestones
- **Garage Brief:** a weekly evidence-backed summary (built; live delivery not yet exercised)
- **Resilience:** durable retry/backoff for email, idempotent sends, per-user rate limits, and scheduled retention (30-90 days)

## Why I built this

Watching car creators describe how long it took to find the car they wanted made it clear the bottleneck is evidence, not search: knowing which listings are real, available, and priced clearly. Jamanyo sits between "I know exactly what I want" and "I know how I want to feel about it," and it never asks for your marketplace passwords or browser cookies.

## Tech stack

```
Backend:     Convex (queries, mutations, actions, crons, HTTP webhooks)
Auth:        @convex-dev/auth (Password + email confirmation via AgentMail)
Hosting:     @convex-dev/static-hosting
Rate limit:  @convex-dev/rate-limiter
Scraping:    Firecrawl (search, scrape, Monitors)
Email:       AgentMail (Svix-signed webhooks, threaded replies)
LLM:         OpenAI SDK -> NVIDIA NIM endpoint
Frontend:    React 19 + Vite + plain CSS
```

**LLM note:** I use the OpenAI SDK against an NVIDIA NIM endpoint because my OpenAI credits ran out. Nothing else needs to change to run an OpenAI model, and I'll switch when credits are refilled.

## Challenges we ran into

- **A closed auction read as a live bid.** The model treated the final price on a closed Bring a Trailer page as a current bid. I added a deterministic override so a source-declared closed or sold state beats model output.
- **Market pages are not listings.** Broad searches returned category hubs. I built a source registry that routes queries to canonical market routes and passes only direct listing pages to verification.
- **Structured output on NVIDIA NIM.** NIM doesn't support

```
json_schema
```

, so I built bracket-balanced JSON extraction as the primary path.
- **Provider contracts.** AgentMail rejected my semantic idempotency keys, so I now encode them only at the provider boundary, which keeps retries deterministic.

## Results and metrics

- 34 regression tests passing;

```
npm audit --omit=dev
```

clean
- **Live E46 M3 validation:** 12 sources screened and 0 promoted (10 were generic or market pages, 2 couldn't be inspected). This validated the false-positive gate, and it also showed that discovery needs to target direct listing pages.
- **Email round trip (development):** an inbound email created a guided mission, a threaded reply was sent, and a repeat webhook delivery was deduplicated.
- **Production:** signup with email confirmation, sign-in, and demo inbox provisioning verified end to end.
- **Not yet verified on production:** candidate emails going out, private inboxes for other users (waiting on an AgentMail plan upgrade), and live Firecrawl Monitor callbacks.

## What's next

Open per-user inboxes on an upgraded AgentMail plan, run production on an OpenAI model, and add direct-listing enumeration for more sources.

title: ClaimHero
description:
ClaimHero turns insurance denials into cited appeals with policy research, missing-proof detection, and human-approved delivery.





## The problem

Insurance denials do not have a letter problem. They have a traceability problem.

The denial arrives in one document, the insurer’s policy lives somewhere else, supporting clinical evidence is buried in records, the deadline is running, and the appeal destination may not be obvious. By the time someone connects all of that, the case is already harder than it needed to be.

ClaimHero keeps those pieces together in one live case workspace.

## How ClaimHero works

Start with a denial letter, EOB, PDF, image, pasted text, or synthetic demo case. ClaimHero extracts the procedure, denial reason, codes, disputed amount, payer, and appeal deadline.

Digital documents are parsed in the browser, and scanned documents can use local OCR, keeping raw documents away from unnecessary external processing.

Next, ClaimHero finds the insurer’s own Clinical Policy Bulletins and relevant clinical sources. Firecrawl maps insurer domains, discovers policy pages, captures the relevant clauses, and persists the source material in Convex.

The evidence workspace puts the denial beside:

- The insurer’s policy requirement
- Supporting clinical documentation
- Missing evidence
- Conflicting source information
- Relevant precedents
- Source citations and visual proof

The case then moves into Appeal Studio. OpenAI extracts structured facts from de-identified text, embeds precedent queries, and drafts the prose of the appeal. The advocate can inspect the Markdown source, edit the brief, preview the formatted document, review citations, and save versions.

Finally, Payer Dispatch lets the advocate review the recipient, letter, exhibits, and delivery route before anything is sent. AgentMail transmits the approved packet, records delivery identifiers, receives payer replies through signed webhooks, and routes those replies back to the same case.

AI may prepare, classify, cite, and recommend. A human approves every outbound message.

## Evidence instead of unsupported AI output

Every important claim in the appeal must point back to an inspectable policy, clinical, statutory, or precedent source.

The Visual Proof Archive preserves what the insurer’s policy looked like when it was checked, including the wording and date. If the policy page changes later, the case still contains the source evidence the advocate relied on.

ClaimHero’s **Evidence Coverage & Precedent Match Score** is a readiness checklist, not a prediction that an appeal will win. It evaluates:

- CPB and indication alignment
- Clinical documentation and step therapy
- ERISA procedural standing
- Precedent match and legal parity

If live policy or precedent evidence is unavailable, the case becomes provisional and is capped at 40 until a human acknowledges the limitation.

## Why we built it

We wanted to build something useful for a high-stakes workflow where generic AI answers are not enough.

ClaimHero helps patients, family advocates, and denial teams understand why a claim was denied, identify what evidence is missing, prepare a defensible appeal, and keep the process reviewable from denial through final transmission.

It is not a prediction engine and it is not just an AI letter generator. It is a reactive case system built around evidence, deadlines, source integrity, and human review.

## Technology

- **Convex** — reactive database, authorization, durable workflows, vector search, file storage, crons, collaboration, audit history, and realtime UI updates.
- **Firecrawl** — insurer policy discovery, clinical policy crawling, source capture, policy drift checks, and payer intake-route discovery.
- **OpenAI** — de-identified structured extraction, precedent embeddings, and cited appeal drafting through the Convex agent component.
- **AgentMail** — approved appeal transmission, delivery tracking, signed inbound webhooks, payer reply routing, and follow-up correspondence.
- **React, TypeScript, Vite, and TailwindCSS** — the frontend workspace and precision medical interface.
- **pdf.js, Tesseract, and optional AWS Textract** — local document extraction and optional table enhancement.

## Challenges

The hardest parts were not making an AI draft appear. They were:

- Handling unavailable or changing external policy sources without fabricating evidence
- Keeping raw patient information out of model prompts
- Anchoring statutory clocks to the adverse determination date
- Preserving policy screenshots and source provenance
- Routing payer replies back to the correct case
- Supporting live background workflows and realtime updates
- Blocking dispatch when evidence or human approval is missing

## Metrics and demo

The repository currently includes **1,304 automated tests across 83 suites** covering workflows, authorization, OCR and redaction, privacy boundaries, Firecrawl and AgentMail integrations, precedent scoring, deadlines, audit chains, collaboration, provisional evidence gating, and dispatch safety.

The demo cases are synthetic and visibly labelled, but they still run live extraction, crawling, scoring, and drafting rather than displaying mocked results.

[Watch the demo video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M04LMuJRilg)

title: Carter
description:
Curious about what you want. Relentless about finding it.





## How the app works

You chat with Carter about what you're looking for. Carter asks a short clarifying question (often as tappable reply chips), saves your preferences, then searches Amazon, Etsy, and specialty stores you choose—including stores discovered via Firecrawl. Results show up as product cards in chat and a Findings panel. Like or pass teaches Carter what to bring next; save products you think you want to buy to shopping lists. On a schedule, Carter checks the products you added and emails you when prices drop.

## Notable features

- Curious shopping agent with streaming chat and preference memory
- Reply chips for quick clarifying answers without typing everything
- Like / pass on findings so future searches skip rejects and lean into likes
- Per-query search scope: Amazon, Etsy, Discover stores, and custom domains
- Shopping lists with price-drop digests via AgentMail
- Multi-conversation sessions, Lists page, and mobile-friendly context panel
- Auth with Better Auth (email + Google), verification, and account deletion

## Why did you build this

I've tried using current AI models for getting product recommendations and have had mixed results- the models themselves weren't great about getting up to date accurate details. When I learned about FireCrawl, I realized that it could help solve this problem. I think has E-Commerce has become too big for traditional UX to work- there's just too many products out there for users to search through. Often times product decisions come more from exhaustion vs what users actually want. I believe that AI Agents are the future of E-Commerce since they don't get exhausted and can be personalized to a user's needs easily. Carter is my first attempt on creating what I think that solution should look like.

## Tech stack list

- **Frontend:** React 19, Vite, TypeScript, React Router
- **Backend:** Convex (queries, mutations, actions, HTTP actions, crons)
- **AI:**

```
@convex-dev/agent
```

, OpenAI GPT-4o-mini via Convex AI Gateway
- **Auth:**

```
@convex-dev/better-auth
```

(email/password + Google OAuth)
- **Search / scrape:**

```
@firecrawl/firecrawl-convex
```

- **Email:**

```
@agentmail/convex
```

(auth mail + price digests)
- **Hosting:**

```
@convex-dev/static-hosting
```


## Challenges we ran into

- **Firecrawl credit burn:** Early search+scrape drained credits fast. We switched to metadata-first search, capped detail enrich, preferred free open-web fetch when possible, and split searches per domain with site: bias so specialty stores aren't crowded out by Amazon.
- **AgentMail from parent actions:** Component create/send couldn't see AGENTMAIL\_API\_KEY, so auth and digest delivery had to call AgentMail's HTTP API from parent actions.
- **Teaching without friction:** Like/pass, reply chips, and Discover-stores chips had to feel instant in the UI while still feeding structured prefs and search scope back into the agent for the next turn.
- **Cron fairness at scale:** Digests and open-query rechecks needed fair rotation (lastCheckedAt / lastEmailedAt) so a few busy lists don't starve everyone else.
- **Ownership hardening:** Agent tools and list/mail APIs needed session ownership and verified-email locks so client-supplied IDs couldn't cross user boundaries.

title: Compari
description:
Price quoting made easy



I wanted an app that would simplify finding a vendor for me. Lots of jobs like tree cutting, catering or photography require emails and specific details to be able to get an actual quote. Compari takes out all the leg work by doing the searching and contacting for you.

It runs on a Convex backend, once the user has made a request it uses OpenAI models to determine what additional details are required to get accurate pricing from a vendor. After that it will use Firecrawl to search the web for potential matches. An llm will then vet each option individually and automatically exclude any that do not fit the criteria that it had collected earlier. It then presents the user with options that they can choose to contact. The chosen vendors are then contacted using Agent Mail to handle the coordination.

It turned out to be somewhat difficult to get responses from vendors and there probably needs to be a follow up mechanism set up that allows for more emails to be sent if you are not getting responses from the Vendors selected.

title: Faultline
description:
Your landlord told the city it's fixed. Is it? Say so in your own words; we keep it dated and tell you if the city agrees. **Try it in 30 seconds, with no email and no sign-in: [https://clear-dogfish-72.convex.site/try](https://clear-dogfish-72.convex.site/try)** Press the first button. Then pick how you want to answer: type it, say it, talk to it, or let it ring your phone. Under each of your messages the page says how it was read: by the keyword reader with no model, or by GPT-6 Astra, with the tool it finished on and what the run cost. ## The problem In New York City, when a landlord certifies to the housing agency (HPD) that a repair is done, the violation closes after 70 days unless HPD sends an inspector back. A tenant may challenge the certification, but **the city's file holds only the landlord's word. It has no place for the tenant's.** In the 30 days to 15 September, owners certified 7,313 repairs and the city stamped 1,527 certifications FALSE or INVALID. These are different violations, not a rate, and both counts come from one query on the city's own file. That file, like every government file of its kind, is overwritten in place. Yesterday's version is gone. ## One rule, four ways in **The rule: a model never writes a sentence you read, and never decides what is recorded on its own.** GPT-6 Astra may only choose one of twelve tools. The tools write every reply, in words the service already uses. Everything below is a different door onto that same rule. 1. **Write.** Email ``` ASK 155 Linden Boulevard, Brooklyn ``` to **[getnotice@agentmail.to](mailto:getnotice@agentmail.to)**, or type it at /try. Seconds later: each repair the owner certified there that is still inside its 70 days, in the city's words, with the day the 70 days run out. Answer ``` #19114297 STILL BROKEN ``` and no model runs at all. Answer _"the tiles by the compactor are still cracked"_ and **GPT-6 Astra on the OpenAI Agents SDK** reads it and must finish by calling a tool. The tool that records an answer refuses a violation number you were never asked about. 2. **Say it.** Press Say it and answer out loud. OpenAI writes your words down, the recording is dropped, and the words go through the same door as typing. Every reply has a Listen button, and what it reads is what the tool wrote. 3. **Talk to it.** Press Talk to it and **gpt-live-1** becomes the voice, listening and speaking at once over WebRTC. It is told it knows nothing about any building or law. When you ask for something it hands your words to the same door (client delegation), the tools write the reply, and the reply is handed back for the voice to say. A conversation is the one place a model may rephrase what you hear, so the page says what is true: the written reply is the record, the voice is not. The server ends every conversation at 2:30, whatever the page does. 4. **Let it ring you.** Write your own number and **CALL-E** places a real phone call that says at once it is automated and that you asked for it, then puts the same questions to you by voice. When you hang up, **two readers go over the call separately**: CALL-E, which held the conversation, and GPT-6 Astra, which is never shown what CALL-E made of it. An answer is recorded only where the two agree. Where they differ, nothing is recorded and you are asked again in writing. A quote is kept only if the transcript has you saying it. Say you never asked for the call and that number is never rung again. The number itself is not kept: a hash for the limits, and four digits so you can see which phone will ring. Then the part no other door changes: - **Your record.** A private page keeps what the city's file said when we asked, what it says now, HPD's 70 days and your answer, each dated. Under it is every reply we sent you and whether it arrived, from AgentMail's delivery events. - **The city's second word.** When HPD later stamps that certification FALSE or INVALID, you're told, with both dates. Only then does the building's public page say someone said so first, and never in your words. Underneath is a versioned record of **ten government files** (NYC housing violations, NYC restaurant inspections, and eight states' layoff notices), read on a schedule, compared row by row, and kept like a repository. Email a company name and get back what it filed, including the versions the state has since overwritten. | Send this | You get back | | --- | --- | | ```
ASK
``` | Every certified repair still inside its 70 days | | a sentence, typed or spoken | Your answer, kept and dated beside the city's record | | ```
CALL ME +1 718 555 0142
``` | Your phone rings; two readers must agree before anything is recorded | | a company name | Every layoff notice it filed, against the statute that applies | | ```
FOLLOW
``` | One email a day at most, when anything you follow changes | | ```
STOP
``` | Nothing, ever again. Honoured before every other rule | | ```
PACK
``` | A PDF evidence pack, every version hashed with its capture time | | ```
CSV
``` | Every filing as a spreadsheet for a lawyer | | ```
KEEP https://…
``` | That page held as it was served, with a screenshot and a SHA-256 | | ```
FIND
``` | Every page on the open web that names them, the first one held | ## Notable features - **Two readers, or nothing.** A phone call ends in a transcript and in what the calling agent says it heard. One model summarising another model's conversation is how a wrong answer gets recorded with confidence, so Faultline makes them disagree in the open: GPT-6 Astra reads the transcript blind, a pure function compares the two, and only agreement is recorded. On the first real call all three answers agreed; the second reading took five seconds and cost 1.76 cents. - **Which repair you mean is decided by your words, not the model's guess.** The city's description of every question is embedded when we ask; your sentence is embedded when you answer; a **Convex vector index** filtered to your address says which question your words are nearest. If the model picked a different number, nothing is recorded: we ask. We found this one by running it. On 17 September the live inbox filed _"the latch on the compactor closet door is still broken"_ against the plexiglass at the building entrance. The same sentence now asks which repair you mean. - **A model can pick the wrong tool, but it cannot ring a number nobody wrote.** The call tool checks that the digits to be rung appear in the person's own message. One number is rung at most twice a day, and one switch stops every call without a deploy. - **A public trial with fences.** /try needs no account, so anyone can open it and a script can open a thousand. It pays at the door from rate-limit rooms of its own (the Convex rate limiter component), so nothing typed or spoken into a browser can spend the inbox's replies or its agent runs; it cannot follow or be emailed; and what is said in a trial is never counted as a tenant's word on a public page. - **Private by default.** A tenant's words never reach a public page. - **Firecrawl as a second witness.** Wisconsin's page is read through Firecrawl, with its own git-diff and a full-page screenshot kept beside our diff. When the two disagreed, Firecrawl's diff showed why: only a ``` ?version=N ``` number on the state's links had moved, a number we had already stopped quoting. - **The components are the agent's hands.** Send a link and Firecrawl holds the page as served. Name an owner and Firecrawl search finds what the open web says about them. Ask for proof and the evidence pack or spreadsheet arrives as an AgentMail attachment. - **The inbox is a working surface.** Every message is labelled in AgentMail with how it was read and what came of it, so what's still unread is what nothing has handled. A bounce or spam complaint stops the mail and takes the follows off with it. - **A build log with one entry per commit, corrections included.** ## Why I built it Rights tools usually start from what the law says. The city already records what happened (who certified what, and when the city disagreed), and then overwrites it. Faultline starts from that record, keeps every version of it, and adds the one word the file has no place for: the tenant's, dated. Plenty of the people that word belongs to would rather say it than type it, and some cannot type it at all, so there are four doors and one rule behind them. ## Tech stack - **Convex** is the whole backend: 33 tables, 67 indexes plus full-text and vector search, 181 functions by ``` npx convex function-spec --prod ``` (56 queries, 83 mutations, 27 actions, 15 HTTP actions), 8 crons and the scheduler, file storage, realtime queries, Convex Auth and static hosting. The phone call's card and the live conversation's bar are ordinary realtime queries: the page never polls. **Four components**: static hosting, AgentMail, Firecrawl, and the rate limiter, which holds one counter per ceiling instead of counting tables. Tested with convex-test. - **OpenAI:** GPT-6 Astra on the Agents SDK twice over (the inbox agent with twelve strict tools, tool choice required, a byte-stable cached prefix, a cost ledger in cents and a daily cap; and the blind second reader of every phone call); **gpt-live-1** over WebRTC with client delegation, and a server-side attach that closes every session at the time limit; gpt-4o-mini-transcribe and gpt-4o-mini-tts for Say it and Listen; gpt-5.6-luna for forwarded letters and photographed notices with one zod schema; text-embedding-3-small; moderation; hosted web search. - **AgentMail:** the inbox; the component's verified webhook and event store; delivery events that are acted on; labels on every message; attachments in and out. - **Firecrawl:** the Convex component, with scrape, change tracking in git-diff mode, full-page screenshots, and search. - **CALL-E:** one API call carrying the script the tools wrote and a strict result schema whose violation enum holds only the numbers this person was asked about; an unsigned webhook that is believed for nothing but a call id, with the call read back using our own key. - **Photon:** the same inbox by text, through the Spectrum SDK behind an HMAC-signed webhook. ## Challenges - **The first real phone call hung up on its own.** The greeting ended on "if you did not ask for this call, say so now". A person who did ask has nothing to say to that, so he waited for a question, and the voice took ten seconds of silence for nobody being there. No test could find it, because a stand-in for a phone line never waits for anyone. The opening now asks nothing and runs straight into the first repair, and one silence no longer ends a call. The third call ran 1 minute 58 and recorded three answers. - **A transcriber drops the first word.** The first live conversation heard "Ask about 155 Linden Boulevard" as "About 155 Linden Boulevard", and looked up a company by that name. An address said any of the ways people say one is now read as a request to be asked about it. - **A Convex component can't read the app's environment.** Replies moved onto the AgentMail component's send queue failed in production, so they went back to direct sends within minutes. The component still verifies the webhook and passes on delivery events. - **A city file is bigger than one transaction**, so each read commits in slices of 150 rows between a start and a finish. - **The free plan's database reads.** Convex bills the whole document read, not the fields a query returns. Re-checking the housing file every hour to learn nothing had changed cost about 6 MB a read; opening one file's commit log cost about 9 MB; and the landing page read 237 rows to show three lines. Each read now fingerprints its rows and skips the comparison when nothing moved, every commit keeps its own tally, and the landing reads one 3.8 KB row. - **Being wrong in public.** We read Wisconsin's ``` ?version=N ``` numbers as revision counts; we withdrew that claim, and Firecrawl's own diff later confirmed the correction. For a day the live site's pages talked to the dev deployment after a hand-built redeploy. Both are in the build log with their fixes. ## Metrics - 10 government files read on a schedule, **2,625 reads** by 19 September; 17,368 NYC housing records and 6,736 restaurant inspection rows held. - Since 29 August: **14,497 rows added, 18,717 edited in place** with the before and after kept, and **105 deleted from the source and still held**. - ASK answered 2.2 s after sending; a reply marked delivered 2.4 s after it was sent; an answer in plain words handled by GPT-6 Astra for about 2.4 cents. - The browser trial, from a browser with no cookies: ASK answered in 1.6 s with no model; a sentence in plain words read by GPT-6 Astra and recorded against the right repair in 8.7 s. - A live conversation on production (20 September): the three repairs were handed to the voice 1.4 s after it asked; a spoken answer was read by GPT-6 Astra and put on the right one of three repairs for 2.41 cents; 142 seconds of gpt-live-1 cost 11.83 cents. - A real phone call on production (20 September): 1 minute 58, three answers, the blind second reading agreed on all three in 5 seconds for 1.76 cents. - **360 automated checks**: 149 engine, 111 receipt, 38 state, 10 wall and 9 markdown checks, plus 43 convex-test tests, and a copy lint over every user-facing string. Nothing in a test can ring a telephone. - **182 commits and 92 build-log entries** since 30 August. **Try it:** in a browser at [https://clear-dogfish-72.convex.site/try](https://clear-dogfish-72.convex.site/try), or email ``` ASK 155 Linden Boulevard, Brooklyn ``` to [getnotice@agentmail.to](mailto:getnotice@agentmail.to) and answer the reply in a sentence. title: Duebell
description:
Peru gives companies 15 business days to answer a consumer complaint. Duebell keeps the clock, reads the reply and drafts your filing.





## Problem you're solving

In Peru, a company has 15 business days to answer a formal consumer complaint, with no extension. Most people never count those days, many replies say nothing concrete, and by the time someone notices, the deadline has passed and they do not know how to escalate to Indecopi, the consumer protection agency.

## How the app works

1. You file your complaint in the company's complaint book and give Duebell's inbox as your contact email.
2. **Convex** starts the legal clock in Lima business days and schedules a check for the end of the deadline day.
3. **AgentMail** receives the company's reply through a signed webhook.
4. **OpenAI** classifies the reply as a commitment, a resolution or stalling, and must quote the sentence it relied on.
5. **Firecrawl** reads Indecopi's public sanctions registry, which has no API.
6. If the company stalls or the deadline passes, Duebell drafts the Indecopi filing in Spanish, with an English copy to read.

## Notable features

- A recorded case plays on the home page in 44 seconds.
- **Try it live** runs the real loop in about 30 seconds, with a demo control that moves the calendar so the scheduled check fires.
- The model never moves the clock: deadlines are plain TypeScript.
- Private sessions with Convex Auth, and live updates through Convex queries.

## Why did you build this

People in Peru lose real money to complaints that quietly expire. The law already protects them; what is missing is someone keeping the clock and turning a non-answer into a ready filing.

## Tech stack list

- Convex: queries, mutations, actions, scheduled functions, HTTP actions, Convex Auth, static hosting, components
- AgentMail (

```
@agentmail/convex
```

)
- OpenAI (strict JSON schema output)
- Firecrawl (browser actions)
- React, TypeScript, Vite, 45 tests

## Challenges we ran into

- Indecopi's registry is a JavaScript app with no API, so Firecrawl drives it like a browser and a parser structures the result.
- Keeping the AI honest: a quote that does not appear in the original email is discarded.
- Letting judges watch a 15 business day deadline pass in seconds without faking the scheduler.

## Any success stories or metrics

title: Exorcist
description:
Find what is haunting your card. Forward your receipts and it cancels what you forgot about.





### The problem

Everyone is paying for something they have forgotten about. The hard part was
never deciding to cancel — it is finding out what you are paying for at all, and
then getting through a cancellation process that is deliberately awkward. The
policy is buried, and some services only accept email or a web form.

### How it works

1. You get an inbox address. Forward anything that says "your subscription
renewed".
2. It reads the _original_ receipt inside the forward rather than the envelope,
so forwarding straight from Gmail works, and extracts the merchant, amount,
cadence and next renewal date.
3. The ledger builds itself, with a running annual total.
4. Pick something and it goes and reads that merchant's own cancellation page,
works out whether it can be cancelled by email, and drafts the letter.
5. You approve it. The confirmation comes back to the same inbox, is read, and
the row flips — with the money you have freed going up.

### Notable features

- Reads forwarded mail properly: the original sender is inside the body, not the
envelope, which is where naive parsers get this wrong.
- Cancellation procedures are cached per merchant and shared, so a merchant
looked up once is instant afterwards and never re-crawled.
- Nothing is cancelled without you approving the letter.
- Renewal timeline with a warning before anything charges you again.
- Where a service cannot be cancelled by email, it shows the real steps and the
form URL instead of pretending.

### Why I built it

I genuinely did not know what was charging my card, and finding out by reading a
year of statements is exactly the kind of task that should not require a human.

### Tech stack

Convex (database, live queries, mutations, actions, HTTP actions, scheduler,
crons, Convex Auth, the Agent component, static hosting), OpenAI, Firecrawl,
AgentMail, React, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind.

### Challenges

Routing inbound mail when the sender is unknown. A forwarded receipt arrives from
your address, about a merchant, with no thread to attach to — so it routes by
registered sender first, then by thread for replies, then by a short per-user
code as a fallback for addresses it has never seen.

Also: making the crawl budget survive public traffic. The guard checks the
provider's real credit balance before spending and refuses below a reserve, so
the pool cannot be drained by a stranger clicking around.

title: Quote Arena
description:
Post a home repair job once. It finds contractors, emails them all, and ranks what comes back.





### The problem

Getting three quotes for a fence or a roof means finding contractors, writing the
same email eight times, and then trying to compare eight replies that price
things completely differently. One quote includes disposal, another does not
mention it. One says two weeks, another says nothing at all.

### How it works

1. You post the job once — trade, description, photos, city.
2. It searches the web for local contractors, reads their sites, and pulls out
the business, its services and a contact address.
3. You pick who to contact. It emails them all from one inbox, with the photos.
4. Replies come back and are turned into the same shape: price range, timeline,
earliest start, what is included, what is excluded, and — just as usefully —
what the contractor never mentioned.
5. The leaderboard reorders live as quotes land.

### Notable features

- The ranking is transparent and shown in the UI:


```
price midpoint × (1 + 1% per day of timeline) × (1 + 3% per unstated field)
```

.
- It charges a quote for being vague. A cheap price with no dates does not
automatically win — an unstated timeline is assumed to be 21 days. In the demo,
$2,900 with no dates scores $3,614 and loses to a $3,200–3,600 quote at $3,468;
the same $2,900 wins at $2,958 once it states two days.
- A revised quote from the same contractor supersedes the old one.
- Contractor questions get a proposed answer drawn from the job facts, which you
approve before it sends.
- "Not stated" is displayed as a first-class value rather than hidden.

### Why I built it

The comparison is the actual work, and it is the part nobody does properly,
because it means reading eight emails carefully and building a table by hand.

### Tech stack

Convex (database, live queries, mutations, actions, HTTP actions, scheduler,
crons, file storage with upload URLs, Convex Auth, static hosting), OpenAI,
Firecrawl, AgentMail, React, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind.

### Challenges

Getting the leaderboard reorder to be a real layout animation rather than a
re-render — it was verified frame by frame, about 520ms of spring transform with
overshoot.

The subtler one was resisting the urge to make the cheapest quote win. The first
version of the demo narration claimed it did, and the app disagreed — correctly,
because the quote had no timeline. The app was right and the script was wrong.

description:
When someone dies there are forty companies to tell. After finds each process, writes the letters, and tracks them. # After _The letters, forms and follow-ups that come after a death — found, written and tracked, so a family doesn't have to._ 🌐 **[Live demo](https://kindred-guanaco-234.convex.site/)** (example estate: [Robert's accounts](https://kindred-guanaco-234.convex.site/e/demo-robert)) · 🎥 **Demo video:** [Watch the demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eZ8eIKz-_tc) · 📓 **[Build log](https://vibeapps.dev/s/hackathon.md)** > The demo runs on the free tiers of Convex, OpenAI, Firecrawl and AgentMail, so under load some features may be rate-limited — the video shows the full flow. ## What this is After is a small web app for the week after someone dies. You tell it a first name, a date, and how you were related. Then you name the companies that need to know — the bank, the phone company, two streaming services, the insurer — and it finds each company's own instructions for a deceased account holder, writes a plain letter to each one, and keeps track of what comes back. It is not a legal service and it does not touch anyone's money. It handles the correspondence, which is the part that is mostly typing. ## The problem A death leaves behind something like forty accounts. Each company has a different process, buried on a different page under a different name — "bereavement", "deceased customer", "estate services". Each wants a slightly different document. Each reply arrives days later, in its own thread, in an inbox that is already full. The work is not hard; it is long, repetitive, and it lands on someone in the worst week of their life, usually while they are also arranging a funeral. ## Our solution In the order you meet it: 01. **Three questions.** A first name, the date, and your relationship. That is all we keep about the person who died — no address, no account numbers, no last name. You are signed in anonymously, so there is no account to make. 02. **Name the companies.** A checklist by category (bank, phone, utilities, streaming, social, insurance, government), plus a box for anything else. Add as many as you like. 03. **After finds the real procedure.** For each company it searches the web, keeps only results on the company's own domain, picks the page that is actually about deceased account holders, reads it, and turns it into a few plain steps: what they need, who to write to, how long they usually take. The card on the board says what it is doing while it does it — _finding their page_, _reading their instructions_, _writing the letter_. 04. **A letter is drafted for each one.** Short, calm, factual, in the voice of a family member. It says "died", not "passed away". It names the documents that company asked for. It is signed with the relationship only. 05. **You read it, change anything, and press Send.** **Nothing is ever sent without that press.** The draft sits in "Ready to send" until a person approves it. You can edit the text and the recipient, or ask for a rewrite. 06. **Replies come back to the board.** Each letter goes out from one inbox with a short case code in the subject. When a company answers, the reply is matched back to the exact card, summarised in one sentence, and the card moves: _Waiting_, _Needs something_, or _Done_. 07. **Quiet companies get a nudge.** After a week of silence, a follow-up is drafted and left waiting for approval — again, never sent on its own. One nudge per company, by design. 08. **Today.** Each morning the board picks at most three things worth doing, with a sentence at the top that does not push. "Three small things. You don't have to finish this today." 09. **Share it with a sibling.** The board is one link. A second person opens it, joins, and sees the same cards move in real time, with a quiet indicator of who else is looking. 10. **Ask After.** A panel that answers "what does the bank still need from me?" using only this estate's own cards and research. ## How we used each sponsor | Sponsor | What it does in After | Where in the code | | --- | --- | --- | | **Convex** | The whole app: database, live board, background pipeline, email webhook, crons, file storage, auth, components — and it serves the frontend | ```

Nothing polls. When a background action patches a card, every open board redraws. - **Mutations** — ``` estates.create ``` , ``` estates.join ``` , ``` tasks.addMany ``` , ``` tasks.updateDraft ``` , ``` tasks.setStatus ``` , ``` tasks.redraft ``` , ``` tasks.prepareDocumentsReply ``` , and the human gate, ``` tasks.approveAndSend ``` . Send and status changes use ``` withOptimisticUpdate ``` ( ``` src/components/TaskDetail.tsx ``` ) so the card moves the instant you click. - **Actions** — the three sponsor SDKs run in ``` "use node" ``` actions only ( ``` convex/research.ts ``` , ``` convex/ai.ts ``` , ``` convex/send.ts ``` , ``` convex/mailActions.ts ``` , ``` convex/inbound.ts ``` , ``` convex/ask.ts ``` ). No API key is ever in the browser bundle; there is no ``` VITE_ ``` -prefixed secret. - **HTTP actions** — ``` convex/http.ts ``` routes Convex Auth's endpoints, the AgentMail webhook at ``` /api/agentmail/webhook ``` (Svix signature verified with Web Crypto in ``` convex/lib/svix.ts ``` ), and registers static hosting last as the catch-all. - **Scheduler** — the whole pipeline is ``` ctx.scheduler.runAfter ``` . ``` tasks.addMany ``` schedules research per company; ``` research.lookup ``` schedules the draft; ``` tasks.approveAndSend ``` schedules the send; the webhook stores the message through ``` mail.ingest ``` , schedules the classifier and returns 200 immediately, so a slow model can never cause a webhook retry storm. When the rate limiter says wait, ``` research.lookup ``` reschedules _itself_ with the limiter's own ``` retryAfter ``` . - **Crons** — ``` convex/crons.ts ``` : a daily follow-up sweep ( ``` ai.followUpSweep ``` ) and a daily plan build ( ``` ai.buildAllDailyPlans ``` ). - **File storage** — ``` estates.documentUploadUrl ``` issues an upload URL, ``` estates.attachDocumentFile ``` attaches it to a paper on the checklist, and ``` estates.documents ``` hands back a ``` ctx.storage.getUrl ``` link. - **Convex Auth** — ``` convex/auth.ts ``` registers Anonymous and Password. Opening the live URL signs you in anonymously ( ``` src/auth.tsx ``` ), so a judge meets the app and not a login wall; Password exists for coming back later. ``` requireMember ``` in ``` convex/estates.ts ``` guards every write, and ``` mail.unrouted ``` is restricted to accounts with a real email, because anonymous proves nothing. - **Components** — three, registered in ``` convex/convex.config.ts ``` : ``` @convex-dev/static-hosting ``` serves this React app from the same deployment (the URL above is ``` convex.site ``` , not a separate host), ``` @convex-dev/rate-limiter ``` meters every credit-spending path per user _and_ globally ( ``` convex/lib/limits.ts ``` ), and ``` @convex-dev/agent ``` is the assistant behind **Ask After** — ``` convex/ask.ts ``` creates one thread per estate and stores its id on the estate row, so siblings share one conversation, and ``` convex/assistant.ts ``` reads it back with ``` listMessages ``` as a live query. - **Presence** — a 20-second heartbeat mutation and a ``` viewers ``` query, so you can see when your sister has the board open. **The shared** ``` playbooks ``` **cache.** A company's procedure is looked up once for everybody. ``` tasks.addMany ``` checks ``` by_companyKey ``` before it schedules anything, and ``` research.lookup ``` checks again before it spends a crawl. The first family to add Netflix pays for the research; the second family gets it instantly and for free. ``` tasks.upsertPlaybook ``` refuses to overwrite a real playbook with a generic fallback, so the cache only improves. ### 🔎 Firecrawl ``` convex/research.ts ``` is the whole point of the product, and Firecrawl is what makes it possible. - **Search with content** — ``` search(ctx, " deceased account holder bereavement close account", 5) ``` with ``` scrapeOptions: { formats: ["markdown"] } ``` , so the results arrive with page text already attached and most lookups need no second call. - **Domain filter** — ``` looksOfficial() ``` drops forums, news and complaint sites; only pages on something that looks like the company's own domain survive. - **Scrape** — when the chosen result's text is too thin to extract from, ``` scrape() ``` reads the page to markdown. - **A credit gateway, not a call counter** — every crawl goes through one function in ``` convex/lib/firecrawl.ts ``` that serves a stored result when it has one, checks Firecrawl's own free credit-usage endpoint before spending, refuses to go below a reserve or past a daily ceiling, and records what each call cost in ``` crawlBudget ``` . A refused crawl is not an error: the family still gets general steps and a letter, and the board says plainly that it is showing saved research. The source URL, page title, confidence and fetch date stay on the playbook and are shown on the card, so a family can check where a step came from. ### ✉️ AgentMail Real letters, to real addresses, with real replies coming back. - **One inbox, created once** — ``` mailActions.ensureInbox ``` is idempotent: it looks for an inbox with this app's ``` clientId ``` before creating one, so re-running never burns an inbox. - **Sending** — ``` send.notify ``` → ``` mailActions.send ``` → ``` lib/agentmail.sendMail ``` . The subject carries the estate's case code (e.g. ``` [AFT-DEMO] ``` ), the outbound row is stored in ``` mailMessages ``` with ``` targetId ``` set to the card that sent it, and the returned thread id is stored on the task. - **Fail-closed sending** — outbound mail refuses to leave at all unless the deployment sets either a redirect address for development or an explicit allow-real-sends flag. Nobody emails a real company from a laptop by accident. - **Receiving** — AgentMail posts ``` message.received ``` , ``` message.delivered ``` and ``` message.bounced ``` to ``` /api/agentmail/webhook ``` . The signature is verified before anything is read, ``` mail.ingest ``` de-duplicates by message id (webhooks retry), and routing tries thread id, then the case code in the subject matched against the letter that started the conversation, then a registered sender address. Unroutable mail is kept and surfaced on ``` /admin ``` , never dropped. - **The reply moves the board** — ``` inbound.onInbound ``` classifies the reply as _closed_, _needs documents_, _needs a call_, _auto-reply_ or _other_, writes a one-sentence summary, and patches the card.
